Any unusual behaviour qualifies as a disorder
A disorder is defined solely by its symptoms

questions.explanation: A disorder requires clinically significant distress or impairment, not symptoms alone. Unusual behaviour, symptom-only definitions, and harm-to-others requirements are mistakes.

questions.stem: A common mistake is using absence of harm as the criterion for a disorder; explain why that is wrong

answer.exemplar: A behaviour can be disordered without harming others, and harmless behaviours need not be disorders; the criterion is distress or impairment to the individual, not social harm to third parties

questions.explanation: Absence of harm is not the criterion because a behaviour can be disordered without harming others, and harmless behaviours need not be disorders. The criterion is distress or impairment to the individual.
questions.hint: Harm to others is not the standard

questions.stem: A common mistake is treating statistical deviation as proof of disorder; what can it not say

options.text: It cannot say whether the trait is measurable
It cannot say whether the trait is common
It cannot say whether the trait is harmful
It cannot say whether the trait exists

questions.explanation: Statistical deviation cannot say whether a trait is harmful or impairing. Commonness, measurability, and existence are separate issues that deviation may or may not address.

stimulus.body: A common mistake reads only the first axis; a multi-axis profile shows a clinical syndrome on axis one, a personality condition on axis two, and moderate psychosocial stressors on axis four.

questions.stem: A common mistake reads only the first axis of a multi-axis profile

options.text: The personality and stressor axes add distinct information
Only the clinical syndrome matters for treatment
The extra axes are redundant with the first
Multi-axis profiles are never useful

questions.explanation: The personality and stressor axes add distinct information beyond the clinical syndrome. Reading only the first axis misses clinically relevant factors.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: A Threshold Placed on a Continuous Distribution
questions.learningObjective: Compute the number below a threshold
questions.stem: A common mistake miscounts; 34 of 80 score below the threshold; what proportion
questions.explanation: The proportion is 34 divided by 80, which equals 0.425. Forty-two and a half percent score below the threshold in this sample.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Two Clinicians Judging Sixty Cases
questions.learningObjective: Identify a source of disagreement between raters
questions.stem: A common mistake blames clinician skill; disagreements cluster near the diagnostic threshold

options.text: The clinicians are incompetent
The cases are identical and easy
The threshold is ambiguous near the cut point
Agreement is impossible to improve

questions.explanation: Disagreements clustering near the threshold suggest the cut point is ambiguous there. Incompetence, identical easy cases, and unimprovable agreement are not supported.
questions.hint: Clustered disagreements point to the cut point

questions.topic: Disorders: Agreement Between Raters Is Not Validity
questions.learningObjective: Compute the agreement rate in a reliability study
questions.stem: A common mistake conflates agreement with validity; raters agree on 54 of 60 cases; what is the agreement rate
questions.explanation: The agreement rate is 54 divided by 60, which equals 0.9. Ninety percent agreement indicates high reliability but not validity.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: A Clinic Sample and Why Its Rates Do Not Transfer
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of population prevalence
questions.stem: A common mistake uses clinic samples; design a study of true population prevalence

answer.exemplar: Sample randomly from the community, apply the same diagnostic criteria as in clinics, and compare the resulting prevalence to clinic rates to estimate selection bias

questions.explanation: Random community sampling with the same criteria, compared to clinic rates, estimates selection bias and yields true population prevalence. This corrects the clinic-sample mistake.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Two Stages of Screening With Two Different Thresholds
questions.learningObjective: Compute the positive predictive value of a two-stage screen
questions.stem: A common mistake miscounts; a two-stage screen yields 18 true positives and 2 false positives; what is the positive predictive value
questions.explanation: Positive predictive value is 18 divided by 20, which equals 0.9. Ninety percent of positive screens are true positives in this sample.
questions.hint: Divide true positives by all positives

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Defining a Disorder by Distress and Impairment Rather Than by Symptoms Alone
questions.learningObjective: Identify the core criterion for disorder
questions.stem: A common mistake uses symptoms alone; what is the core criterion for a disorder

options.text: The presence of any unusual symptom
Violation of social norms
Statistical rarity of the behaviour
Clinically significant distress or impairment

questions.explanation: The core criterion is clinically significant distress or impairment, not unusual symptoms, statistical rarity, or norm violation. Those may accompany but do not define disorder.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Why Absent Harm Is Not the Criterion
questions.learningObjective: Design a study testing harm absence as criterion
questions.stem: A common mistake uses harm absence; design a study testing the proper criterion

answer.exemplar: Compare cases with distress or impairment but no harm to others against harmless cases with no distress, and test whether disorder ratings track distress and impairment rather than harm

questions.explanation: Comparing distressed or impaired cases without harm to harmless cases without distress, and testing whether ratings track distress and impairment, directly tests the proper criterion. This isolates the relevant factor.
questions.hint: Vary distress and impairment, not harm

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise statistical deviation and its limits
questions.stem: A common mistake equates deviation with disorder; synthesise a correction

answer.exemplar: Statistical deviation marks rarity, not harm or impairment; a rare trait may be benign and a common trait impairing, so deviation alone cannot define disorder

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: A Threshold Placed on a Continuous Distribution
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a threshold on a well-being scale

stimulus.body: A common mistake reifies a threshold; a well-being score of 49 versus 51 falls on opposite sides of a 50 cut point, but the underlying difference is trivial.

questions.stem: A common mistake reifies a threshold; 49 versus 51 fall on opposite sides of a 50 cut point

options.text: The two scores represent fundamentally different states
The cut point eliminates measurement error
The scores are practically equivalent despite crossing the cut point
Scores near the cut point are perfectly reliable

questions.explanation: Scores of 49 and 51 are practically equivalent despite crossing the cut point. The difference is trivial, so the cut point does not mark a real state change.
questions.hint: Near the cut point, states are similar

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Agreement Between Raters Is Not Validity
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise reliability and validity in a diagnostic context
questions.stem: A common mistake treats agreement as validity; synthesise a correction

answer.exemplar: Agreement indicates raters apply criteria consistently, which is reliability; validity requires the criteria capture the true disorder, needing independent evidence such as outcomes or gold standards

questions.explanation: Agreement indicates consistent criterion application, which is reliability. Validity requires the criteria capture the true disorder, needing independent evidence such as outcomes or gold standards.
questions.hint: Reliability is consistency; validity is truth

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a clinic rate in light of selection bias

stimulus.body: A common mistake generalises clinic rates; a specialty clinic reports 60 percent of patients have a disorder, while the community rate is 10 percent.

questions.stem: A common mistake generalises a 60 percent clinic rate when the community rate is 10 percent

options.text: The clinic rate is the true population rate
The 10 percent rate is impossible
The community survey is certainly wrong
The clinic overrepresents severe cases, inflating the rate

questions.explanation: The clinic rate exceeds the community rate because clinics overrepresent severe cases. The community survey is the better population estimate.
